landscape: Comparative data on bureaucracy are thinner than data on elections or regimes, and they come from three kinds of producers. Academic expert surveys measure the structure and quality of administrations: the QoG Expert Survey, the historical Evans-Rauch Weberianness data and the COCOPS survey of senior executives. International organisations produce statistics and assessments: the World Bank's Worldwide Bureaucracy Indicators and Global Survey of Public Servants, OECD Government at a Glance and SIGMA, PEFA, ILOSTAT, and the UN and OECD digital-government indices. National statistical and personnel agencies publish workforce data, best developed in the United States (FEVS, OPM Federal Workforce Data, ASPEP, Census of Governments).

U.S. agencies have their own set of datasets on agency design, independence, politicization and capacity: the ACUS Sourcebook, Selin's independence scores, Lewis's insulation and appointee data, agency ideology estimates and Bednar's capacity scores. Cross-national agency data are limited to the GlobalReg regulatory-agency datasets. International bureaucracies (UN secretariats, European Commission staff) and party patronage form small niche literatures with few released datasets.

Many measures in this domain are snapshots or have short series. The QoG Expert Survey has three waves (2008-2020), Evans-Rauch covers 1970-1990, and InCiSE was replaced by the Blavatnik Index in 2024. Several promising academic measures (Gilardi's agency independence index, Bauer-Ege's IO autonomy scores, the Commission officials surveys) were never released as data and are not catalogued.

core.text: The QoG Expert Survey asks public-administration experts about recruitment, career stability, impartiality, politicization and other features of each country's bureaucracy. Its third wave (2020) covers 117 countries and its second 158. It is widely used as a cross-national source on Weberian structure and impartiality and links to the wider QoG datasets. There is no wave after 2020, and the number of experts per country varies, so country scores carry different precision.

The Worldwide Bureaucracy Indicators, compiled by the World Bank from household and labour-force surveys, measure the size, composition and relative wages of public employment in 202 economies from 2000 to 2022. They are a broad, comparable source on public-sector employment and pay. Because they rest on survey definitions of public employment, they can differ from administrative headcounts.

The Global Survey of Public Servants harmonises surveys of civil servants' management practices, motivation and attitudes in up to 28 countries, 2010-2022. It is a cross-national source on what happens inside administrations rather than on their formal structure. Reported country and respondent counts conflict across its own documentation, so users should check the files they download.

The Blavatnik Index of Public Administration, launched in 2024 as the successor to the International Civil Service Effectiveness Index, scores the effectiveness of central-government administration in 120 countries from existing data sources. It offers broad coverage but depends heavily on the availability and recency of its inputs.

The Open Budget Survey of the International Budget Partnership measures budget transparency, public participation and oversight in rounds from 2006, covering 125 countries in 2023 and 82 in 2025. It is a widely used comparative measure of fiscal transparency and links budgeting to accountability research.

choosing: Separate three questions: how a bureaucracy is organised (expert surveys such as QoG-ES and Evans-Rauch), how big and well paid it is (WWBI, ILOSTAT, national workforce data), and how well it performs (Blavatnik Index, PEFA, WGI government effectiveness). Indices that blend these, such as WGI and V-Dem public administration, are convenient for long series but cannot tell the mechanisms apart.

For U.S. agencies, formal-design datasets (ACUS Sourcebook, Selin, Lewis insulation) and behavioural or attitudinal data (FEVS, SFGS, agency ideology) can be linked by agency and year, which allows tests that are not possible cross-nationally.
gaps: No regularly updated cross-national panel of bureaucratic structure exists; QoG-ES ends in 2020 and has only three waves.
Cross-national data on agency independence and on political appointments outside the United States and Westminster systems are scarce, and the main regulatory-agency datasets are frozen around 2010.
International bureaucracies are covered only by UN-system personnel statistics, European Commission HR figures and one dataset on UN secretariats; survey data on IO officials have not been released.
